claims.claim: Mitochondrial stress activates immune responses broadly, encompassing target genes of both the Toll and Imd pathways.
claims.source: Activation of immune responses is broad in this case, encompassing target genes of both the Toll and Imd pathways.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on analysis of RNAseq data showing upregulation of immune genes from multiple pathways.

claims.claim: Induction of antimicrobial peptide genes by mitochondrial stress is specific and not triggered by heat shock or ER-UPR activation.
claims.source: We confirmed the induction of several immune genes by quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR), and further demonstrated that transcriptional induction of these genes was specifically triggered by mitochondrial stress and not by conditions that trigger the cytoplasmic- (heat shock) or endoplasmic reticulum (loss of ER-associated degradation after knockdown of Hrd1, (Bordallo et al., 1998)) unfolded protein responses (Figure 1c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in Figure 1c comparing gene induction under different stress conditions, with citation to Bordallo et al., 1998 for ER-UPR methodology.

claims.claim: ΔOTC expression leads to induction of mitochondrial chaperones and proteases associated with the UPRmt.
claims.source: We also used qPCR to confirm that ΔOTC expression leads to induction of mitochondrial chaperones and proteases associated with the UPRmt, under conditions used in earlier studies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claims.claim: Acute ΔOTC expression for 24 hr mildly improves resistance to oral infection with pathogenic Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
claims.source: Resistance to oral infection was mildly increased, while the speed by which flies succumb to humoral infection was unaffected; we speculate that this may be because the modest induction of immune genes is not sufficient to clear bacteria introduced directly to the hemolymph (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by infection survival data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a.

claims.claim: Acute ΔOTC expression does not affect resistance to humoral infection with Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
claims.source: Resistance to oral infection was mildly increased, while the speed by which flies succumb to humoral infection was unaffected; we speculate that this may be because the modest induction of immune genes is not sufficient to clear bacteria introduced directly to the hemolymph (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by infection survival data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a.

claims.claim: Knocking down FoxO blocks induction of metchnikowin by mitochondrial stress.
claims.source: Knocking down the transcription factors foxo and Relish/NF-κB, but not jun or kayak/Fos, strongly suppressed Mtk induction (Figure 1d), consistent with upregulation of several FoxO target genes in our RNAseq data (Figure 1a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in Figure 1d showing reduced Mtk expression with FoxO knockdown.

claims.claim: Knocking down Relish blocks induction of metchnikowin by mitochondrial stress.
claims.source: Knocking down the transcription factors foxo and Relish/NF-κB, but not jun or kayak/Fos, strongly suppressed Mtk induction (Figure 1d), consistent with upregulation of several FoxO target genes in our RNAseq data (Figure 1a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in Figure 1d showing reduced Mtk expression with Relish knockdown.

claims.claim: Knocking down JNK/bsk blocks induction of metchnikowin by mitochondrial stress.
claims.source: Indeed, Mtk induction by mitochondrial stress was significantly impaired in bsk loss-of-function conditions (Figure 1d).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in Figure 1d showing reduced Mtk expression with bsk knockdown.

claims.claim: Knocking down ASK1 blocks induction of metchnikowin by mitochondrial stress.
claims.source: Knocking down ASK1 and PGAM5 blocked induction of Mtk after mitochondrial stress, suggesting that PGAM5, ASK1, and JNK are components of a pathway responsible for transducing mitochondrial stress to downstream transcription factors (Figure 1d).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in Figure 1d showing reduced Mtk expression with ASK1 knockdown.

claims.claim: Knocking down PGAM5 blocks induction of metchnikowin by mitochondrial stress.
claims.source: Knocking down ASK1 and PGAM5 blocked induction of Mtk after mitochondrial stress, suggesting that PGAM5, ASK1, and JNK are components of a pathway responsible for transducing mitochondrial stress to downstream transcription factors (Figure 1d).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in Figure 1d showing reduced Mtk expression with PGAM5 knockdown.

claims.claim: PGAM5 homozygous null mutants do not show induction of metchnikowin after mitochondrial stress.
claims.source: The lack of Mtk induction in PGAM5 homozygous null mutants (PGAM51/1) experiencing mitochondrial stress confirmed this finding (Figure 1d).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in Figure 1d showing lack of Mtk induction in PGAM5 null mutants.

claims.claim: Disruption of the PGAM5-ASK1-JNK pathway blocks induction of classical UPRmt genes such as hsp60 and hsp10.
claims.source: To determine whether this pathway indeed represented UPRmt signaling, we tested and confirmed that its disruption also blocks induction of classical UPRmt genes such as hsp60 and hsp10 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b–d).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b-d showing reduced expression of UPRmt genes when the pathway is disrupted.

claims.claim: Knocking down PGAM5 or ASK1 does not affect induction of antimicrobial peptides following exposure to pathogenic Pseudomonas entomophila.
claims.source: Ubiquitously knocking down either PGAM5 or ASK1 had no effect on this response (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b), suggesting that the pathway mediating AMP induction in response to mitochondrial stress is distinct from the canonical Toll and Imd pathways.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b showing normal AMP induction after pathogen exposure despite PGAM5 or ASK1 knockdown.

claims.claim: The pathway mediating AMP induction in response to mitochondrial stress is distinct from the canonical Toll and Imd pathways.
claims.source: Ubiquitously knocking down either PGAM5 or ASK1 had no effect on this response (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b), suggesting that the pathway mediating AMP induction in response to mitochondrial stress is distinct from the canonical Toll and Imd pathways.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that disrupting the mitochondrial stress pathway does not affect canonical immune responses.

claims.claim: PGAM5 null flies show higher baseline levels of apoptosis.
claims.source: Although PGAM5 null flies showed higher baseline levels of apoptosis, in line with previous reports (Ishida et al., 2012), ΔOTC expression stress did not induce apoptosis in our experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by TUNEL assay data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2c and cited previous work by Ishida et al., 2012.

claims.claim: ΔOTC expression does not induce apoptosis.
claims.source: Although PGAM5 null flies showed higher baseline levels of apoptosis, in line with previous reports (Ishida et al., 2012), ΔOTC expression stress did not induce apoptosis in our experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by TUNEL assay data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2c showing no increase in apoptosis after ΔOTC expression.

claims.claim: Blocking mitochondrial ROS production from complexes I and III does not affect metchnikowin induction after mitochondrial stress.
claims.source: We blocked mitochondrial ROS production from sites on complexes I and III of the ETC using previously characterized compounds (Brand et al., 2016; Orr et al., 2013) but did not see any effect on Mtk induction after mitochondrial stress (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3a and cited methodology from Brand et al., 2016 and Orr et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Overexpression of catalase or jafrac1/Trx-1 during developmental ΔOTC expression does not affect acute or lasting FoxO activation.
claims.source: Along these lines, overexpression of the antioxidant enzymes Catalase and jafrac1/Trx-1 during developmental ΔOTC expression does not affect acute or lasting FoxO activation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b & c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by FoxO localization data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3b and 3c.

claims.claim: Direct activation of ASK1 by ROS is not the basis of ΔOTC-mediated AMP induction.
claims.source: This suggests that direct activation of ASK1 by ROS is not the basis of ΔOTC-mediated AMP induction.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from experiments showing that blocking ROS or overexpressing antioxidants does not affect the response.

claims.claim: The transcriptional response to mitochondrial unfolded proteins in flies is mediated by a pathway involving PGAM5, ASK1, JNK, Relish and FoxO.
claims.source: Together, these data indicate that the transcriptional response to mitochondrial unfolded proteins in flies is mediated by a pathway involving PGAM5 and ASK1, as well as JNK, Relish and FoxO (Figure 1e).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the collective genetic and molecular data presented in Figure 1 and supplements.

claims.claim: Expressing ΔOTC throughout larval development extends median adult lifespan by 21% and maximal lifespan by 14%.
claims.source: To confirm this observation in our system, we used the ubiquitous RU486-inducible daughterless GeneSwitch (DaGS) driver to express ΔOTC throughout larval development only, and measured adult lifespan. As shown in Figure 2a,g—figure supplement 2, this treatment consistently extended maximum and median lifespan.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 2a and Figure 2g showing 21% and 14% increases.

claims.claim: ΔOTC expression limited to adulthood does not extend lifespan.
claims.source: Confirming observations in C. elegans, ΔOTC expression limited to adulthood did not lead to extended lifespan (Figure 2b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by lifespan data in Figure 2b and comparison to C. elegans observations.

claims.claim: The absence of PGAM5 prevents lifespan extension after developmental ΔOTC expression.
claims.source: To determine whether the pathway we identified in the experiments described above is required for this longevity effect, we assessed lifespan in PGAM5 homozygous null flies (Figure 2c). The absence of PGAM5 prevented lifespan extension after developmental ΔOTC expression, suggesting that the protective effects responsible for lifespan extension are downstream of PGAM5.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by lifespan data in Figure 2c showing no lifespan extension in PGAM5 null flies.

claims.claim: FoxO double heterozygous null flies show significantly reduced adult lifespan after developmental ΔOTC expression.
claims.source: In line with this, the adult lifespan of FoxO double heterozygous null flies was significantly reduced after developmental ΔOTC expression (Figure 2d).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by lifespan data in Figure 2d showing reduced lifespan in FoxO heterozygous null flies.

claims.claim: PGAM5 and FoxO nulls show reduced survival through larval development when subjected to mitochondrial proteostatic stress.
claims.source: Both PGAM5 and especially FoxO nulls also showed reduced survival through larval development when subjected to mitochondrial proteostatic stress (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by larval survival data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: FoxO activity plays an integral part in promoting resilience to mitochondrial stress during development.
claims.source: This suggests that FoxO activity plays an integral part in promoting resilience to mitochondrial stress in these conditions.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that FoxO null flies show reduced survival during developmental stress.

claims.claim: Flies given antibiotics throughout adulthood still show lifespan extension by developmental ΔOTC expression.
claims.source: In both cases, we observed increased median and maximal lifespan after developmental ΔOTC expression, just as in flies reared normally (Figure 2e–f).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by lifespan data in Figure 2e showing lifespan extension in antibiotic-treated flies.

claims.claim: Flies raised in sterile conditions from egg stage still show lifespan extension by developmental ΔOTC expression.
claims.source: In both cases, we observed increased median and maximal lifespan after developmental ΔOTC expression, just as in flies reared normally (Figure 2e–f).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by lifespan data in Figure 2f showing lifespan extension in axenic flies.

claims.claim: Larval ΔOTC expression does not affect pathogen resistance at day 7 of adulthood.
claims.source: Larval ΔOTC expression also did not affect pathogen resistance at day 7 of adulthood (Figure 2—figure supplement 3a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by infection survival data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3a.

claims.claim: Developmental ΔOTC expression does not significantly affect intestinal microbiome load at different points of life.
claims.source: We further analyzed the intestinal microbiome load (as assessed by colony-forming units, CFUs) at different points of life after developmental ΔOTC expression, and found no significant difference relative to controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 3b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by CFU quantification data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3b.

claims.claim: Developmental ΔOTC expression does not cause major changes in microbiome composition in young and old flies.
claims.source: To test effects on microbiome composition, we performed 16S sequencing in young and old flies after developmental ΔOTC expression, and similarly found no major changes relative to controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 3c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by 16S sequencing data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3c.

claims.claim: Activation of the immune system following developmental ΔOTC expression does not contribute to the observed increase in adult longevity.
claims.source: Altogether, these data indicate that activation of the immune system following developmental ΔOTC expression does not contribute to the observed increase in adult longevity.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from experiments showing lifespan extension occurs even without microbiome and without changes to pathogen resistance or microbiome composition.

claims.claim: Developmental ΔOTC expression does not affect the ratio of NAD/NADH in adult flies.
claims.source: We first tested the ratio of NAD/NADH, as a measure of mitochondrial function, but did not detect changes in adults after developmental ΔOTC expression (Figure 3a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by NAD/NADH ratio measurements in Figure 3a.

claims.claim: Developmental ΔOTC expression does not change MitoTracker intensity in adult muscle tissue.
claims.source: We also did not see changes in MitoTracker intensity in muscle tissue from adults after developmental ΔOTC expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by MitoTracker intensity measurements in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claims.claim: Expressing ΔOTC during development leads to reduced triglyceride concentrations in adult flies.
claims.source: However, we found that expressing ΔOTC during development leads to reduced triglyceride (TAGs) concentrations (relative to total protein) in adult flies (Figure 3b); this phenotype is consistent with activation of FoxO, which is known to induce lipases and increase fat metabolism (Karpac et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by triglyceride measurement data in Figure 3b and cited work by Karpac et al., 2013.

claims.claim: PGAM5 null mutants do not show a decrease in TAG levels after developmental ΔOTC expression.
claims.source: PGAM5 null mutants did not show a decrease in TAG levels, supporting the notion that this metabolic shift results from UPRmt signaling.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from triglyceride data showing no change in PGAM5 nulls, supporting the role of UPRmt signaling.

claims.claim: ΔOTC expression throughout development leads to increased nuclear localization of FoxO in the fat body of third instar larvae.
claims.source: ΔOTC expression during development strongly induced nuclear translocation of FoxO in late L3 larval fat bodies (Figure 3c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 3c showing FoxO nuclear localization.

claims.claim: PGAM5 null mutant larvae do not show FoxO nuclear translocation after developmental ΔOTC expression.
claims.source: Again, this was not evident in PGAM5 null mutant larvae.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing lack of FoxO nuclear localization in PGAM5 null larvae.

claims.claim: Flies retain nuclear-localized FoxO in adult fat bodies one week after eclosion following developmental ΔOTC expression.
claims.source: To test this, we imaged adult fat bodies one week after eclosion and found that flies retained nuclear-localized FoxO after developmental ΔOTC expression (Figure 3d).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 3d showing persistent FoxO nuclear localization in adults.

claims.claim: Adding the JNK inhibitor SP600125 to larval food inhibits both larval and adult FoxO nuclear translocation.
claims.source: We next tested whether this lasting effect on FoxO was dependent on JNK activity during development, by adding the JNK inhibitor SP600125 to the larval food. This treatment inhibited both larval and adult translocation of FoxO to the nucleus (Figure 3e, left).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 3e showing reduced FoxO nuclear localization with SP600125 treatment.

claims.claim: Expressing dominant negative bsk simultaneously with ΔOTC in adult flies limits FoxO nuclear translocation.
claims.source: Developmental expression of dominant negative bsk (bskDN) was lethal, but expressing bskDN simultaneously with ΔOTC in adult flies limited FoxO nuclear translocation (Figure 3e).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 3e showing reduced FoxO nuclear localization with bskDN expression.

claims.claim: ΔOTC expression for 24 hr on day 3 of adulthood leads to acute but not lasting nuclear translocation of FoxO.
claims.source: We expressed ΔOTC for 24 hr on day 3 of adulthood, which lead to acute but not lasting nuclear translocation of FoxO (Figure 3e, right).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 3e showing FoxO localization after adult treatment.

claims.claim: The absence of a persistent response to mitochondrial stress after adult treatment is consistent with the lack of lifespan extension in these conditions.
claims.source: The absence of a persistent response to mitochondrial stress after adult treatment adults is consistent with the lack of lifespan extension in these conditions (Figure 2b).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred by comparing the lack of persistent FoxO activation with the lack of lifespan extension after adult treatment.

claims.claim: The persistent activation of FoxO in response to developmental UPRmt activation is the mechanism by which developmental but not adult mitochondrial stress can extend lifespan.
claims.source: Our results suggest that the persistent activation of FoxO in response to the developmental activation of the UPRmt is the mechanism by which developmental but not adult mitochondrial stress can extend lifespan.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the collective observations about timing-dependent FoxO activation and lifespan extension.

claims.claim: A large number of genes are upregulated in larvae acutely expressing ΔOTC, predominantly involved in energy metabolism.
claims.source: We observed a large number of upregulated genes in the acutely stressed larvae (Figure 4a; using a minimum baseline FPKM value of 10 and a cutoff of 3-fold induction relative to controls). These genes were predominantly involved in energy metabolism, and showed considerable overlap between the wild type and PGAM5 null mutant data sets.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data in Figure 4a showing upregulated genes and their functional categories.

claims.claim: Only a small number of genes induced by acute larval stress remain upregulated in adult flies, predominantly heat-shock and stress response genes.
claims.source: Only a small number of these (predominantly heat-shock and stress response genes) remained upregulated in adult flies.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data comparing larval and adult gene expression.

claims.claim: None of the genes induced persistently in wild-type flies remain induced in PGAM5 nulls.
claims.source: Notably, none of the genes induced persistently in wild-type flies remained induced in PGAM5 nulls (Figure 4b,c).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data in Figure 4b and 4c comparing wild-type and PGAM5 null flies.

claims.claim: Persistently upregulated genes include twelve chaperones, some of which are FoxO targets and have been shown to extend lifespan when upregulated.
claims.source: These genes include twelve chaperones, some of which are FoxO targets (Donovan and Marr, 2016; Wang et al., 2003) and have previously been shown to extend lifespan when upregulated (Liao et al., 2008; Morrow et al., 2004; Tatar et al., 1997; Wang et al., 2003; Zhao et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data and multiple citations to previous work on FoxO targets and lifespan extension.

claims.claim: The only non-chaperone-encoding genes persistently induced (Tsp42E and Obp99) are regulated by FoxO and involved in lifespan regulation.
claims.source: The only non-chaperone-encoding genes in this list (Tsp42E and Obp99) are also regulated by FoxO and are involved in lifespan regulation (Alic et al., 2014; Bai et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data and citations to Alic et al., 2014 and Bai et al., 2013.

claims.claim: FoxO translocates to the nucleus after developmental ΔOTC expression and remains nuclear after 9 hours of starvation.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 5a, FoxO translocates to the nucleus after developmental ΔOTC expression. After 9 hours of starvation (only water was offered to flies), the fat body of both stressed and control flies exhibit nuclear FoxO.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 5a showing FoxO localization under different conditions.

claims.claim: 24 hr of refeeding resets FoxO activation in control flies but not in flies that experienced developmental stress.
claims.source: 24 hr of refeeding resets this activation in control flies, but FoxO remained nuclear in flies that had experienced developmental stress.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing differential FoxO localization after refeeding.

claims.claim: Switching flies to a pure sucrose diet for 5 days does not abolish persistent nuclear localization of FoxO caused by developmental ΔOTC expression.
claims.source: Further supporting the idea that the mitochondrial proteostatic stress affects FoxO independently of insulin signaling, switching flies to a diet of pure sucrose (5% in water) for 5 days did not abolish the persistent nuclear localization of FoxO caused by developmental ΔOTC expression (Figure 5b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 5b showing FoxO localization on different diets.

claims.claim: Flies switched to a high-protein diet for 5 days show nearly complete loss of nuclear FoxO in the fat body after developmental ΔOTC expression.
claims.source: However, flies switched to an alternate diet containing ~5 x higher protein levels than control food showed a nearly complete loss of nuclear FoxO in the fat body after 5 days (Figure 5b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 5b showing FoxO localization on high-protein diet.

claims.claim: Supplementation with rapamycin at 200 µM prevents the loss of nuclear FoxO on high-protein diet.
claims.source: To test whether this high-protein diet affects FoxO localization through the main amino-acid-sensing pathway mTORC1, we repeated this experiment with supplementation of the mTORC1 inhibitor rapamycin at 200 µM. This prevented the loss of nuclear FoxO (Figure 5b), suggesting that mTORC1 activation can override the persistent nuclear translocation of FoxO produced by developmental ΔOTC expression.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 5b showing FoxO localization with rapamycin treatment.

claims.claim: Activating mTORC1 during developmental stress by RNAi of TSC1 prevents lasting FoxO activation.
claims.source: In support of this role for mTORC1, activating mTORC1 during developmental stress (by RNAi of its inhibitor TSC1) prevents lasting FoxO activation (Figure 5c, left), while reducing developmental survival in the same manner as FoxO deficiency (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 5c and survival data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Simultaneous over-expression of TSC1 and TSC2 to inhibit mTORC1 activity in adult flies is sufficient to promote nuclear translocation of FoxO.
claims.source: Furthermore, simultaneous over-expression of TSC1 and 2 to inhibit mTORC1 activity in adult flies is sufficient to promote nuclear translocation of FoxO (Figure 5c, right).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 5c showing FoxO localization with TSC1/2 overexpression.

claims.claim: Overexpression of GCN-2 is sufficient to induce nuclear localization of FoxO.
claims.source: Indeed, overexpression of GCN-2 was sufficient to induce nuclear localization of FoxO, while knocking down GCN-2 during developmental ΔOTC expression abrogates the lasting effect on FoxO (Figure 5d).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 5d showing FoxO localization with GCN-2 overexpression.

claims.claim: Knocking down GCN-2 during developmental ΔOTC expression abrogates the lasting effect on FoxO.
claims.source: Indeed, overexpression of GCN-2 was sufficient to induce nuclear localization of FoxO, while knocking down GCN-2 during developmental ΔOTC expression abrogates the lasting effect on FoxO (Figure 5d).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 5d showing loss of FoxO nuclear localization with GCN-2 knockdown.

claims.claim: Knocking down GCN-2 in flies treated with rapamycin reduces nuclear FoxO.
claims.source: To test whether GCN-2 acts downstream of mTORC1 in this context, we knocked down GCN-2 in flies treated with rapamycin and observed a reduction in nuclear FoxO (Figure 5e).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 5e showing FoxO localization with combined rapamycin and GCN-2 knockdown.

claims.claim: Developmental ΔOTC expression does not extend lifespan when flies are fed a high-protein diet throughout adulthood.
claims.source: To test this hypothesis, we repeated our lifespan experiment with developmental ΔOTC expression but switched flies to the high-protein diet after eclosion. The high-protein diet reduced the lifespan of the control group relative to our standard fly food, consistent with previous literature, but also completely abolished the lifespan extension normally induced by ΔOTC expression (Figure 5f).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by lifespan data in Figure 5f showing no lifespan extension on high-protein diet.

claims.claim: The UPRmt has been associated with long lifespan across metazoans.
claims.source: The mitochondrial unfolded protein response (UPRmt) has been associated with long lifespan across metazoans.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the UPRmt across different organisms.

claims.claim: In Caenorhabditis elegans, mild developmental mitochondrial stress activates UPRmt reporters and extends lifespan.
claims.source: In Caenorhabditis elegans, mild developmental mitochondrial stress activates UPRmt reporters and extends lifespan.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established findings in C. elegans research.

claims.claim: Developmental mitochondrial stress is necessary and sufficient to extend Drosophila lifespan.
claims.source: We show that similar developmental stress is necessary and sufficient to extend Drosophila lifespan, and identify Phosphoglycerate Mutase 5 (PGAM5) as a mediator of this response.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the lifespan experiments presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: PGAM5 is a mediator of the response to developmental mitochondrial stress that extends lifespan.
claims.source: We show that similar developmental stress is necessary and sufficient to extend Drosophila lifespan, and identify Phosphoglycerate Mutase 5 (PGAM5) as a mediator of this response.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by genetic experiments showing PGAM5 is required for lifespan extension.

claims.claim: Developmental mitochondrial stress leads to activation of FoxO via ASK1 and JNK.
claims.source: Developmental mitochondrial stress leads to activation of FoxO, via Apoptosis Signal-regulating Kinase 1 (ASK1) and Jun-N-terminal Kinase (JNK).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by genetic and molecular experiments showing the pathway components.

claims.claim: FoxO activation persists into adulthood after developmental mitochondrial stress.
claims.source: This activation persists into adulthood and induces a select set of chaperones, many of which have been implicated in lifespan extension in flies.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing persistent FoxO nuclear localization in adults.

claims.claim: Persistent FoxO activation induces a select set of chaperones, many of which have been implicated in lifespan extension in flies.
claims.source: This activation persists into adulthood and induces a select set of chaperones, many of which have been implicated in lifespan extension in flies.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data and citations to previous lifespan studies.

claims.claim: Persistent FoxO activation can be reversed by a high-protein diet in adulthood through mTORC1 and GCN-2 activity.
claims.source: Persistent FoxO activation can be reversed by a high-protein diet in adulthood, through mTORC1 and GCN-2 activity.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing loss of FoxO nuclear localization on high-protein diet and with mTORC1/GCN-2 manipulation.

claims.claim: The observed lifespan extension is prevented on a high-protein diet.
claims.source: Accordingly, the observed lifespan extension is prevented on a high-protein diet and in FoxO-null flies.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by lifespan data showing no extension on high-protein diet.

claims.claim: The observed lifespan extension is prevented in FoxO-null flies.
claims.source: Accordingly, the observed lifespan extension is prevented on a high-protein diet and in FoxO-null flies.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by lifespan data showing no extension in FoxO null flies.

claims.claim: The UPRmt was first described in mammalian cells more than a decade ago.
claims.source: The response was first described in mammalian cells more than a decade ago (Martinus et al., 1996; Zhao et al., 2002) and has since been studied primarily in Caenorhabditis elegans.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on citations to Martinus et al., 1996 and Zhao et al., 2002.

claims.claim: In C. elegans, strong evidence suggests that the UPRmt is involved in delaying aging and promoting adult lifespan.
claims.source: In worms, strong evidence suggests that the UPRmt is involved in delaying aging and promoting adult lifespan (Baker et al., 2012; Durieux et al., 2011; Houtkooper et al., 2013; Merkwirth et al., 2016; Mouchiroud et al., 2013; Tian et al., 2016; Yang and Hekimi, 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on multiple citations to C. elegans studies.

claims.claim: The UPRmt is reminiscent of, but distinct from, the cytoplasmic (heat shock) and endoplasmic reticulum unfolded protein responses.
claims.source: This work has revealed the UPRmt to be reminiscent of, but distinct from, the cytoplasmic (heat shock) and endoplasmic reticulum unfolded protein responses (Baker et al., 2012; Haynes et al., 2007; 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on citations to Baker et al., 2012 and Haynes et al., 2007, 2010.

claims.claim: Through the UPRmt, mitochondrial stress induces a nuclear transcriptional response that promotes the expression of mitochondrial chaperones and proteases.
claims.source: Through the UPRmt, mitochondrial stress induces a nuclear transcriptional response that promotes the expression of a group of mitochondrial chaperones and proteases (Aldridge et al., 2007; Yoneda et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on citations to Aldridge et al., 2007 and Yoneda et al., 2004.

claims.claim: The primary transcription factor in C. elegans UPRmt is ATFS-1.
claims.source: The primary transcription factor in C. elegans is ATFS-1, which is regulated by membrane potential-dependent import into and degradation in mitochondria (Nargund et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on citation to Nargund et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Mitochondrial stress blocks ATFS-1 import and ATFS-1 instead moves to the nucleus where it interacts with DVE-1 and UBL-5 to turn on the transcriptional response.
claims.source: Mitochondrial stress blocks this import and ATFS-1 instead moves to the nucleus, where it interacts with DVE-1 and UBL-5 to turn on the transcriptional response (Benedetti et al., 2006; Haynes et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on citations to Benedetti et al., 2006 and Haynes et al., 2007.

claims.claim: The UPRmt response includes a metabolic reconfiguration to increase glycolytic capacity while restoring oxidative phosphorylation.
claims.source: In addition to proteostatic elements, this response includes a metabolic reconfiguration to increase glycolytic capacity while restoring oxidative phosphorylation (Nargund et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on citation to Nargund et al., 2015.

claims.claim: A separate branch of the UPRmt mediates a general downregulation of translation through GCN-2 and eIF2α.
claims.source: Meanwhile, a separate branch of the UPRmt mediates a general downregulation of translation, through GCN-2 and eIF2α (Baker et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on citation to Baker et al., 2012.

claims.claim: In mice, perturbation of mitochondrial translation has been implicated in long lifespan.
claims.source: In mice, perturbation of mitochondrial translation has been implicated in long lifespan (Houtkooper et al., 2013), and recent findings have revealed the conservation of the ATFS-1 regulated transcriptional response (mediated by ATF5 in mice (Fiorese et al., 2016)).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on citations to Houtkooper et al., 2013 and Fiorese et al., 2016.

claims.claim: The ATFS-1 regulated transcriptional response is conserved in mice and mediated by ATF5.
claims.source: In mice, perturbation of mitochondrial translation has been implicated in long lifespan (Houtkooper et al., 2013), and recent findings have revealed the conservation of the ATFS-1 regulated transcriptional response (mediated by ATF5 in mice (Fiorese et al., 2016)).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on citation to Fiorese et al., 2016.

results.result: Mitochondrial stress induced by ΔOTC overexpression or ND75 knockdown activates a transcriptional response enriched for stress signaling, chaperones/proteases, and innate immune genes. This response is specific to mitochondrial stress and not triggered by heat shock or ER-UPR.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 collectively demonstrate a specific mitochondrial stress response through RNAseq and qPCR validation (C1-C2), with appropriate specificity controls comparing heat shock and ER-UPR (C4). The overlap analysis (C1) and functional enrichment (C2-C3) provide converging evidence for a core UPRmt signature.

results.result: The transcriptional response to mitochondrial stress in Drosophila requires PGAM5, ASK1, JNK, Relish, and FoxO. Genetic disruption of any component blocks induction of both antimicrobial peptides and classical UPRmt genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C14 and C22 provide systematic genetic evidence using RNAi knockdowns and null mutants showing each pathway component is required for the stress response. The data include both AMP reporters (C8-C13) and classical UPRmt genes (C14), demonstrating pathway completeness.

results.result: The PGAM5-ASK1-JNK pathway mediating mitochondrial stress responses is distinct from canonical Toll and Imd immune pathways and does not contribute to lifespan extension through improved immune function.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C16 show that disrupting the mitochondrial stress pathway does not affect canonical pathogen responses, while C34 integrates multiple lines of evidence (antibiotic treatment, axenic conditions, pathogen resistance, microbiome analysis) demonstrating immune activation is not responsible for longevity effects.

results.result: ΔOTC expression does not induce apoptosis, though PGAM5 null flies show elevated baseline apoptosis consistent with prior reports.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C18 are supported by TUNEL assay data and appropriate citation to previous work. This control experiment rules out apoptosis as a confounding mechanism for the observed stress responses.

results.result: ROS production is not required for mitochondrial stress-induced AMP expression, as blocking mitochondrial ROS or overexpressing antioxidants does not affect the response.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C21 use both pharmacological ROS inhibitors and genetic antioxidant overexpression to demonstrate ROS-independence. The experiments appropriately cite methodology and provide converging negative results ruling out direct ROS-mediated ASK1 activation.

results.result: Developmental ΔOTC expression extends Drosophila lifespan by 21% (median) and 14% (maximum), while adult-only expression has no effect, demonstrating developmental timing is necessary and sufficient for longevity.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C24 and C65 present lifespan data with appropriate controls showing developmental specificity. The consistent extension across multiple experiments and comparison to C. elegans findings strengthen the conclusion about developmental timing requirements.

results.result: PGAM5 and FoxO are required for lifespan extension by developmental mitochondrial stress, with both null mutants showing loss of longevity benefits and reduced survival during developmental stress.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C28 provide genetic loss-of-function evidence in both lifespan and developmental survival assays. The data demonstrate both PGAM5 and FoxO are necessary for the longevity phenotype, with FoxO showing stronger developmental survival defects consistent with its downstream role.

results.result: Lifespan extension by developmental mitochondrial stress occurs independently of the microbiome, as shown by experiments with antibiotics, axenic conditions, and lack of changes in pathogen resistance or microbiome composition.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C33 systematically rule out microbiome contributions using multiple complementary approaches: antibiotic treatment (C29), axenic rearing (C30), pathogen resistance assays (C31), CFU quantification (C32), and 16S sequencing (C33). The convergence of negative results strongly supports microbiome-independence.

results.result: Developmental ΔOTC expression reduces adult triglyceride levels in a PGAM5-dependent manner without affecting NAD/NADH ratios or mitochondrial content, consistent with FoxO-mediated metabolic changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C38 characterize metabolic phenotypes with appropriate controls. The PGAM5-dependence of TAG reduction (C38) links the metabolic change to the identified signaling pathway, while negative results for NAD/NADH and MitoTracker rule out general mitochondrial dysfunction.

results.result: Developmental ΔOTC expression induces FoxO nuclear translocation in larval fat bodies that persists into adulthood in a PGAM5-dependent manner.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C41 and C68 use immunohistochemistry to demonstrate FoxO activation during development and persistence in adults. The PGAM5-dependence (C40) links FoxO activation to the upstream signaling pathway, providing a mechanistic connection to longevity.

results.result: Persistent FoxO activation requires JNK activity during development, as shown by pharmacological and genetic JNK inhibition. Adult-only mitochondrial stress produces transient but not lasting FoxO activation, explaining the lack of lifespan extension.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C46 demonstrate developmental timing requirements for persistent FoxO activation using both JNK inhibitor (C42) and dominant-negative genetics (C43). The comparison to adult treatment (C44-C45) directly links persistent FoxO activation to longevity outcomes.

results.result: Developmental mitochondrial stress induces acute metabolic gene expression in larvae, but only a small subset of genes (predominantly chaperones and FoxO targets) remain upregulated in adults in a PGAM5-dependent manner. Many of these persistently induced chaperones have been previously implicated in lifespan extension.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C51 and C69 use RNAseq to identify persistently upregulated genes with appropriate PGAM5 null controls. The identification of FoxO target chaperones with prior longevity associations provides mechanistic insight, though the reliance on literature citations for lifespan effects of individual genes is a limitation.

results.result: Persistent FoxO activation after developmental stress is independent of insulin signaling but can be reversed by high-protein diet through mTORC1 activation. Rapamycin prevents this reversal.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C56 and C70 use starvation/refeeding experiments and dietary manipulations to dissect FoxO regulation. The sucrose diet control (C54) rules out insulin signaling, while the high-protein diet and rapamycin experiments (C55-C56) implicate mTORC1 in a novel regulatory mechanism.

results.result: mTORC1 and GCN-2 regulate persistent FoxO activation, with TSC1/2 overexpression sufficient to induce FoxO nuclear localization and GCN-2 acting downstream of mTORC1 to promote FoxO activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C61 use genetic manipulations (TSC1 RNAi, TSC1/2 overexpression, GCN-2 overexpression/RNAi) to establish an mTORC1-GCN-2-FoxO regulatory axis. The epistasis experiment with rapamycin and GCN-2 RNAi (C61) supports the proposed pathway order.

results.result: High-protein diet throughout adulthood completely abolishes lifespan extension from developmental ΔOTC expression, consistent with the requirement for persistent FoxO activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C62 and C71 demonstrate that dietary intervention can override developmental programming. This result directly links the molecular mechanism (FoxO activation) to the physiological outcome (longevity) and has important translational implications.

results.result: Acute ΔOTC expression for 24 hours mildly improves oral infection resistance but does not affect humoral infection resistance.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7 are supported by infection survival data, though the speculation about insufficient AMP induction for humoral infections is not directly tested. The differential effects on oral vs. humoral infection suggest route-specific immune modulation.

results.result: The manuscript contextualizes findings within established UPRmt literature across species, citing prior work on transcriptional responses, metabolic reconfiguration, epigenetic regulation, and developmental timing requirements.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C95 represent background knowledge and literature citations that appropriately frame the current work. These claims rely on cited references and established knowledge rather than new experimental data.

results.result: Prior literature establishes PGAM5 as a mitochondrial phosphatase that interacts with ASK1 and PINK1, regulates cell death pathways, and is cleaved upon loss of membrane potential.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C104 summarize prior work on PGAM5 with appropriate citations. These background claims provide context for the current findings but do not represent new experimental results.

results.result: Recent work in C. elegans has identified roles for histone methylation and chromatin remodeling in UPRmt-mediated longevity, though UPRmt reporters correlate poorly with longevity outcomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C108 cite recent literature on epigenetic mechanisms and limitations of UPRmt reporters. These provide important context for interpreting the current findings about persistent gene expression changes.

results.result: Prior work has shown that the UPRmt triggers innate immunity, FoxO can induce Relish signaling, rapamycin activates the UPRmt, and mTORC1 regulates longevity through FOXO in C. elegans.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C113 cite relevant prior work that supports the plausibility of the current findings and provides comparative context across species. These background claims appropriately frame the discussion.
